{{short description|American biologist}}
{{one source|date=March 2013}}
'''Terry Lamon Yates''' (March 17, 1950&nbsp;– December 11, 2007) was an American [[biologist]] and [[Academic staff|academic]] who is credited with discovering the source of the [[hantavirus]] in the [[American Southwest]] in 1993.<ref name=bg>{{cite news |first=Matt |last=Schudel |title=Terry Yates, 57; biologist found source of hantavirus |url=http://archive.boston.com/bostonglobe/obituaries/articles/2007/12/24/terry_yates_57_biologist_found_source_of_hantavirus/ |work= [[Washington Post]] |publisher=[[Boston Globe]] |date=2007-12-24 |access-date=2007-01-04}}</ref> Yates' specialty as a biologist was the study of [[rodents]] and other small mammals.<ref name=bg/>

==Early life==
Terry Yates was born in [[Mayfield, Kentucky]].<ref name=bg/> He earned his [[bachelor's degree]] from [[Murray State University]] before completing his [[master's degree]] in [[biology]] from [[Texas A&M University|Texas A&M]] in 1975. He later received his doctorate in biology from [[Texas Tech University]] in 1978.<ref name=bg/>

==Hantavirus==
Residents living in the [[Four Corners]] region, which encompasses parts of [[Arizona]], [[Colorado]], [[New Mexico]] and [[Utah]], began to experience a mysterious illness in the spring of 1993.<ref name=bg/> The then unknown [[virus]] killed 32 people in just a few weeks, and sickened many others.<ref name=bg/> The illness was originally nicknamed "[[Virus sin Nombre|Sin Nombre]]," after a New Mexican [[canyon]] where [[Spain|Spanish]] settlers massacred [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]] during the colonial era.<ref name=bg/>

Terry Yates, a [[professor]] at the [[University of New Mexico]], joined an interdisciplinary [[research]] team charged with finding the source of the mysterious illness by the National Science Foundation.<ref name=bg/> Yates, along with his research assistant, [[Robert Parmenter]], isolated the source of the illness, which became known as the [[hantavirus]], by using animal [[Biological specimen|specimens]] which he had collected throughout the American Southwest.<ref name=bg/> Yates found that the hantavirus was carried by the [[deer mouse]], a species which had a higher than usual population in early 1993 due to unusually wet weather in the region.<ref name=bg/> The discovery of the hantavirus' origin by Yates has helped to save lives and warn residents about the risks of the disease.<ref name=bg/> The virus has killed more than 125 people between 1993 and 2007.<ref name=bg/>

Yates spent the later years of his life studying the connection between wet [[weather pattern]]s and deer mice populations.<ref name=bg/>

The [[National Science Foundation]] named Yates' discovery of the cause of the hantavirus as one of the top fifty projected funded by the NSF which had the greatest impact on peoples' lives.<ref name=bg/>

==University of New Mexico==
Yates was affiliated with the [[University of New Mexico]] for 29 years before his death in 2007.<ref name=bg/> He served as a professor of  biology and [[pathology]], before becoming the UNM's [[vice president]] for research and economic development, a position he held until his death.<ref name=bg/>

Additionally, Yates directed the National Science Foundation's Division of [[Environmental Biology]] from 1990 to 1992 and again from 2000 to 2001.<ref name=bg/> In 2006, he was appointed to the [[board of directors]] on [[life sciences]] of the [[United States National Research Council|National Research Council]] of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=bg/>

==Death==
Yates lived in [[Placitas, Sandoval County, New Mexico|Placitas, New Mexico]].<ref name=bg/> He died of [[cancer]] on December 11, 2007, at the [[University of New Mexico Hospital]] in [[Albuquerque, New Mexico]], at the age of 57.<ref name=bg/>

In 2017, a recently discovered species of the [[Oligoryzomys]] genus (O. yatesi) was named after him as an homage for his "important contribution to the Chilean mammalogy research".<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/321532465|title=Systematics of Oligoryzomys (Rodentia, Cricetidae, Sigmodontinae) from southern Chilean Patagonia, with the description of a new species|last1=Eduardo Palma|first1=R|last2=Rodríguez-Serrano|first2=Enrique|date=2017-12-01}}</ref>
In 2014, a new species of subterranean rodent from South America was named after Dr. Yates which is called Yates's tuco-tuco, ''Ctenomys yatesi'' [https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/parasitologyfacpubs/722/ Gardner et al., 2014]<ref>Gardner, Scott L.; Salazar-Bravo, Jorge; Cook, Joseph A. (17 June 2014). "New Species of ''Ctenomys'' Blainville 1826 (Rodentia: Ctenomyidae) from the Lowlands and Central Valleys of Bolivia"</ref><ref>Leslie Reed (18 July 2014). "Gardner leads discovery of four new tuco-tuco species". UNL Today. University of Nebraska–Lincoln. Retrieved 21 July 2014.</ref><ref>Carson Vaughan (17 July 2014). "Found: 4 New Species of Gopher-Like Mammals". National Geographic. Retrieved 21 July 2014.</ref>
